text: AI technological abundance (ATA) denotes a regime of strong cost compression and capability expansion in AI-intensive production, in which the marginal cost of many AI-mediated services falls sharply once systems are trained, deployed, and scaled.

AI economic abundance (AEA) denotes a strictly stronger, distributional and institutional outcome: broad affordability of an essential living-standards bundle, which requires that the gains from cost compression pass through to household living standards rather than being captured as rents by owners of scarce bottlenecks.
binding constraints (inputs or permissions that cannot scale without congestion, rationing, or rising shadow prices)

section: From cost compression to living standards
text: We refer to Point A as the regime boundary at which these mechanisms become scalable and persistent rather than episodic. Past Point A, a large and economically meaningful set of AI-intensive services can be supplied at very low marginal cost, so that cost compression becomes a structural feature of production in those domains. Point A is not a single milestone such as AGI; it is a deployment threshold at which models, tools, and robotic systems become reliable enough and cheap enough that many tasks can be executed at scale, and the binding constraints begin to shift away from cognition toward the complements required to deliver services in the real economy.
We define the scarcity structure of an economy as the configuration of binding constraints that shape production, allocation, and distribution at a given point in time.
post-AI bottlenecks (layers where scarcity remains binding)
In short, institutions are the rules; jurisdictions are the territorial entities that give those rules coercive force and geopolitical weight.
